messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 64
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Middle Eastern
  relationship_status: Divorced
  occupation: Politician
  trauma_type: Relief worker in war zone
  pcl5: 45

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Stranger Interaction: Talking to strangers, Military Topics: Talks about military, Olfactory Danger Cue: Burnt smell
  Maladaptive Strategies: Emotion Control: I try hard to control my emotions, Distraction: I distract myself with something else, Overworking: I throw myself into work or tasks to keep my mind occupied
  Threat: Threat in Silence: Unusual silence makes me feel something dangerous is about to happen, Door and Lock Checking: I repeatedly check that doors and windows are locked, Scanning for Danger: I constantly scan my surroundings for signs of danger
  Memory: Terror on Recall: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time, Fragmented Pieces: My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together, Overwhelm on Recall: When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Amir, a 64-year-old state congressman, presents as a man of immense public composure, his tailored suits and measured speech a testament to a long career in politics. Yet, beneath this carefully constructed exterior is a profound and unceasing state of alert that has governed his life for decades. The origin point is his time as a young relief worker in the Middle East, an experience he rarely speaks of but which replays in his mind not as a narrative, but as a series of sensory assaults. He doesn't remember the day of the bombing as a sequence of events; instead, his memory offers only disconnected pieces that refuse to form a whole. There is the memory fragment of the unusual, deadening silence just before the marketplace was hit, a silence so complete it felt like the world holding its breath. Then comes the smell of burnt plastic and scorched earth, a scent that can ambush him now from a backyard barbecue or a city fireplace. He remembers the dust, thick and choking, and the disembodied sounds of screaming, but not the faces of the people he was trying to help. When these fragments surface, they bring with them not just sadness, but the same raw, animal terror he felt then, an emotional wave so powerful he feels it might drown him, forcing him to immediately stop what he's doing and find a distraction.

For years, his political career served as that distraction. Amir threw himself into his work with a relentless energy that colleagues mistook for ambition. In reality, it was a desperate flight from the quiet moments. He learned that as long as he was drafting legislation, attending committee meetings, or preparing for a debate, his mind was occupied. Overworking became his primary strategy for survival. This devotion to his job, however, came at a cost. His ex-wife, he recalls, used to say he was a ghost in their home, present in body but absent in spirit. He couldn't explain to her that the silence of their evenings was not peaceful for him; it was menacing, a vacuum that his mind would rush to fill with the whine of incoming mortars. The marriage eventually dissolved under the weight of his emotional unavailability, a consequence he accepted with a sense of grim inevitability.

Now, living alone, his routines are rigid and defensive. Before he can even think of sleeping, he must perform a meticulous ritual of checking every window and door in his apartment, sometimes two or three times, convinced he has missed something. In public, his political role places him in the path of his most potent triggers. During town hall meetings, he finds himself unable to focus on the person speaking. Instead, he constantly scans the room, cataloging exits, assessing the posture of strangers in the audience, his body tensing at any sudden movement. He has come to believe that danger is always imminent and that only his vigilance keeps it at bay. Talking to constituents, a core function of his job, has become an exercise in extreme self-control. He forces a smile and a firm handshake while his mind races, interpreting every unfamiliar face as a potential threat. Any mention of military affairs, a frequent topic in his line of work, sends a jolt of ice through his veins, threatening to shatter his composure. He grips the podium tighter, focusing on the grain of the wood, trying with all his might to keep his emotions from showing on his face.

What has finally brought Amir to seek help is a growing sense of exhaustion. The constant vigilance, the endless work, the decades of holding his breath have worn him down. Last month, during a televised debate, an opponent brought up foreign military aid, and for a terrifying moment, Amir felt the memory fragments rise with such force that he completely lost his train of thought. The silence stretched on, and in that void, he was back in the dust and the noise. He managed to recover, but the incident terrified him. He is afraid of losing control, of the carefully built walls finally crumbling in public. More than that, he is tired of being at war in his own mind. He hopes, he stated quietly in his first session, to one day be able to sit in a quiet room and feel peace instead of peril.
